title: New York State Senate Asks Governor to Proclaim August 15 as India Independence Day
excerpt: Resolution J1935 celebrates Indian-American contributions as the diaspora's political footprint in New York deepens
body:
The New York State Senate has adopted Resolution J1935, formally asking Governor Kathy Hochul to proclaim August 15, 2026, as India Independence Day across the state. The move, sponsored by Senator Jeremy Cooney of Rochester, drew bipartisan support and warm remarks from senators who praised India's civilizational heritage, democratic traditions, and the growing influence of Indian Americans in New York.

The resolution is the latest in an annual tradition, but this year's debate carried particular weight. With hate crimes against South Asian Americans rising sharply in recent months and political rhetoric around immigration growing more hostile, several senators used the floor discussion to explicitly affirm the belonging of Indian-origin communities in the state.

## A Parade of Praise on the Senate Floor

"Across the globe, Indians are making lasting impacts in their communities, and this is an opportunity to join together and celebrate and reflect on our shared history, culture, and heritage," said Senator Cooney, whose 56th District in western New York is home to a growing Indian-American population drawn by the region's university towns and tech corridor.

Senator Joseph P. Addabbo Jr. invoked Mahatma Gandhi: "Gandhi once said that the future depends on what we do in the present. That message is inspiration even for Indian Americans today and for future generations too."

Senator John C. Liu, representing northeast Queens — home to one of the largest Indian populations in the Western Hemisphere — was even more pointed: "India has been around for thousands of years. It has been a civilization. It has been a country. It has been a model of democracy for actually a lot longer than our country."

Senator Jeremy J. Zellner called Indian Americans "woven into the fabric of our everyday life" in his 61st District, while Senator Steven D. Rhoads credited the community's "culture, traditions, entrepreneurship, and community spirit" for strengthening neighborhoods across the state.

## The Numbers Behind the Recognition

New York is home to over 500,000 Indian Americans, the largest concentration in the Western Hemisphere. The community's educational attainment is striking — 71 percent of Indian Americans in the US hold a bachelor's degree, compared to 32 percent nationally. Indian Americans also lead in household income, entrepreneurship, and representation in medicine, with roughly 35,000 Indian-American physicians practicing nationwide.

The state has been at the forefront of recognizing this influence. In recent years, the legislature has also marked Indian Republic Day, Indian American Heritage Month, and the 75th anniversary of the Indian Constitution. Senator Cooney himself has emerged as one of the most consistent champions of Indian-diaspora recognition in Albany.

The Consulate General of India in New York expressed "sincere gratitude" for the resolution and thanked the senators for their "warm recognition of India's rich heritage and the invaluable contributions of the Indian-American community."

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs in the tri-state area, the resolution is more than ceremonial. It signals growing institutional acknowledgement of a community that has long punched above its political weight in economic and academic spheres but is only now building commensurate political infrastructure.

Organizations like Indian American Impact have been working to translate community wealth and educational achievement into elected seats and policy influence. The bipartisan tenor of the Senate debate — with senators from both parties competing to praise the diaspora — suggests that Indian Americans are increasingly seen not as a niche constituency but as a civic force that both parties want to court.

August 15 will mark India's 79th Independence Day. If Governor Hochul signs the proclamation, it will be one of the most visible state-level recognitions of the date anywhere in the United States.
